\chapter{Please}
\label{ch:ar-please}
\hlchaptermodality{6}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can attach min faḍlik to a request in Arabic and change its ending for a man or a woman.}

Say min faḍlik with the heavy ḍād, take it apart as 'from your grace', and offer law samaḥt as the alternative.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[\ar{من} \ar{فضلك}]{\ar{من} \ar{فضلك} (min faḍlik) — please}

\label{lesson:AR-C06-min-fadlik}



\begin{quote}
Arabic doesn't say \textquotedblleft{}please\textquotedblright{} — it asks for something \emph{from your grace.}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — The phrase}
\textbf{\ar{من} \ar{فضلك}} — read right to left, \textbf{min faḍlik} — is two pieces:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ar{من}} (\emph{min}, \textquotedblleft{}from\textquotedblright{}) + \textbf{\ar{فضلك}} (\emph{faḍl} + \emph{-ik/-ak}, \textquotedblleft{}your grace/bounty\textquotedblright{}) $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{from your grace.}\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\emph{faḍl} is a warm, weighty word — \textquotedblleft{}grace, favour, bounty, generosity\textquotedblright{} (you'll meet it as the name \emph{Faḍl}). Saying \emph{min faḍlik} casts the request as drawing on the other person's generosity — not a command, a courtesy.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens — A gender note (Arabic marks \textquotedblleft{}you\textquotedblright{})}]
The ending changes with \textbf{whom you address} — and, unwritten, only the vowel moves:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item to a \textbf{woman}: \emph{min faḍl\textbf{ik}} (the \ar{ك} said \emph{-ik})
  \item to a \textbf{man}: \emph{min faḍl\textbf{ak}} (the \ar{ك} said \emph{-ak})
\end{itemize}

The spelling \textbf{\ar{فضلك}} is the same for both; the short vowel that distinguishes them isn't normally written. One sound to respect: the \textbf{\ar{ض}} (\emph{ḍ}) is an \textbf{emphatic} d, said with a heavier, deeper tongue than a plain \emph{d}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — Another everyday \textquotedblleft{}please\textquotedblright{}}
Just as common, especially getting someone's attention:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ar{لو} \ar{سمحت}} — \emph{law samaḥt} — literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{if you permit}\textquotedblright{} (\emph{law} \textquotedblleft{}if\textquotedblright{} + \emph{samaḥt} \textquotedblleft{}you permitted\textquotedblright{}). Same politeness, a different image — permission rather than grace.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}min faḍlik\textquotedblright{} — feel the heavy \ar{ض}
  \item taken apart — \textquotedblleft{}from your grace\textquotedblright{}
  \item the alternative — \textquotedblleft{}law samaḥt\textquotedblright{} = \textquotedblleft{}if you permit\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How do you say please in Arabic? (\textbf{min faḍlik}, \ar{من} \ar{فضلك}.) What does it literally mean? (\textquotedblleft{}\textbf{From your grace}\textquotedblright{} — \emph{faḍl} = grace/bounty.) What changes between saying it to a man vs a woman? (The \ar{ك} ending — \emph{-ak} to a man, \emph{-ik} to a woman; spelling unchanged.) What's the other common \textquotedblleft{}please,\textquotedblright{} and what does it mean? (\textbf{law samaḥt} — \textquotedblleft{}if you permit.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
